prize_parts.citation: for the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis

statement.case_for: After reading the openings I have moved my first place from halide perovskites (B045) to massively parallel sequencing (B017). Four of eight members ranked it, three placed it first, and no colleague argued it is immature or conceptually thin. The principle is clear and can be explained to a broad audience: reversible terminators, fluorescent nucleotides and surface-clustered single-molecule templates turn nucleotide chemistry into a parallel readout. This is a physically and chemically defined capability that cut sequencing cost by orders of magnitude and opened population genomics and clinical diagnostics, which is the generative, previously unforeseen opportunity I look for. It has been confirmed for two decades on independent platforms. Within the Solexa lineage the original discovery is separable from later refinements, which makes a defensible three-name citation possible: Balasubramanian and Klenerman for the sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry and Mayer for the clustered colony-array concept.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the serious weakness. Rothberg (pyrosequencing and semiconductor sequencing) and Ju (terminator chemistry) have genuine competing claims, and a three-person cap leaves out at least two people whom many would regard as pioneers. There is also a fit question: Sanger sequencing was honoured in 1980, and parts of the impact belong to physiology or medicine, so some will call this an incremental technology advance rather than a chemical discovery. A citation worded as 'massively parallel sequencing by synthesis' would need to exclude the 454 route explicitly, which a reader may find arbitrary.

responses.point: Aili ranks B017 first with Balasubramanian and Klenerman only, calling the Cambridge Solexa chemistry the most coherent core claim and a two-person award the cleanest.
responses.response: I agree that the Cambridge pair is the coherent core and that a clean citation matters. I still lean towards including Mayer, because clonal clustering on a surface is what makes the readout massively parallel rather than just single-molecule, and that is separable from the terminator chemistry. If the committee cannot settle the Mayer priority from the record, I would accept two names. I do not agree that the narrower list removes the Rothberg and Ju problem; it only makes the exclusion more visible, so the citation wording has to carry that weight.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks B017 first with Balasubramanian, Klenerman and Mayer, and ranks perovskites last on the shortlist because he sees operational stability and commercial viability as unproven.
responses.response: His three-name configuration matches mine, which is reassuring but not independent proof of correctness. On perovskites I partly concede: my opening rated maturity too generously, and stability and lead toxicity are not a minor caveat for a prize based on lasting consequences. I would still separate the discovery of the absorber class, which is firmly reproduced, from the commercial outcome, so I keep B045 as an alternative rather than dismissing it. Where I press him is on Mayer: what evidence supports his priority over Ju or Rothberg?

responses.point: Somfai puts only B048 (Pd-catalysed C-N coupling, Buchwald and Hartwig) on his ranking, calling it complementary to the 2010 cross-coupling prize and mature.
responses.response: This is the cleanest attribution on the table, and I take his point that it is a method everyone uses. My reservation is the generative-novelty test: the 2010 prize already honoured Pd cross-coupling as a principle, and amination is a refinement of that bond-forming logic, albeit a very important one. I would like him to say what new capability, as opposed to a better ligand set, the committee would be citing. I keep B048 as an alternative because its attribution is far less contested than B017.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular condensates (B029) first for bringing phase-behaviour thinking into cell biology, and puts perovskites and B067 lipid nanoparticles lower.
responses.response: I find the physical-chemical framing of condensates attractive and close to my own interests. My concern is maturity and what was actually discovered: Aili and she both note ongoing debate about which cellular structures are truly phase separated and what the function is. I would want that settled before a citation can say more than 'liquid-like organisation'. Compared with sequencing, the empirical basis is less quantitative, so I keep it behind B017 this year, but I do not think it is far behind.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B017 first with the Cambridge pair, and puts genetic-code expansion (B013) second as a mature, conceptually clear chemical tool.
responses.response: I agree on B017 and consider the maturity argument decisive. On B013 I agree it is original and general, but I find it harder to explain to a broad audience, and the trimming from Schultz, Wang, Chin, Mehl and Yokoyama is as arbitrary as in sequencing. It is a credible later candidate, not the right answer in this configuration.

uncertainties: Whether Mayer's clonal-array priority is strong enough to justify a third name over Ju or Rothberg, or whether a two-person Balasubramanian and Klenerman prize is more defensible.
Whether the citation can be worded to credit sequencing by synthesis without appearing to arbitrarily exclude the pyrosequencing and semiconductor routes.
Whether the committee regards DNA sequencing as chemistry, given Sanger in 1980 and its role in medicine.
How much weight perovskite stability should carry against the reproducibility of the absorber discovery.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. None of the shortlisted candidates is at Lund or in NanoLund, and my own work on thermoelectrics, ratchets and molecular motors does not overlap with any shortlisted discovery. I note only that Somfai and Sparr are Lund colleagues, which is not a conflict.
